Open G tuning chord chart

In Open G tuning (D G D G B D), the open strings already make a G major chord. A barre across one fret gives you a major chord, which is why Open G is loved for slide guitar and for rhythm parts in blues and rock.

How to tune to Open G

From standard tuning (E A D G B E), lower three strings by a whole step (2 semitones). The 4th, 3rd, and 2nd strings stay the same.

  • 6th string: E → D (down 2 semitones)
  • 5th string: A → G (down 2 semitones)
  • 1st string: E → D (down 2 semitones)

The open strings ring as G/D (a G chord with D in the bass). If you start a strum from the 5th string, you hear G with G in the bass.

One-finger major chords

Because the open strings make a major chord, laying one finger (or a slide) across all strings at any fret gives another major chord: the 5th fret is C and the 7th fret is D. With G at the open strings, that is the I, IV, and V chords of the key of G — enough for many songs.

Basic chords

These are the first shapes the app finds for each chord, mostly up to the 4th fret. The black dot is the lowest note; the letters in the dots are the intervals (R is the root). “x” means do not play that string.

About G: the app's G (x 0 0 0 0 0) leaves out the 6th string so that G is the lowest note. In practice, strumming all six open strings (G/D, with D in the bass) is the most common way to play G in Open G; the low D is part of its sound.

Tips

  • Watch the 6th string. It is tuned to D, not G. For a G chord with G in the bass, start from the 5th string, or play the 6th string only when D in the bass sounds right.
  • Minor chords need more fingers. The open strings are major, so minor chords such as Em and Am take a shape of their own. The app shows several for each.
  • Other keys: with a capo at the 2nd fret the same shapes play in A; at the 3rd fret, in Bb.
